discovery: Programmable arrays of individually trapped Rydberg atoms for quantum simulation and quantum computation
subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum simulation
motivation: The nominees turned the strong, long-range interactions of Rydberg atoms into a controllable quantum resource. Saffman (and, independently, Browaeys with Grangier) first demonstrated Rydberg blockade between two single atoms in optical tweezers (2009), and Saffman realised the first neutral-atom entangling CNOT gate. Lukin, who co-proposed the dipole-blockade mechanism, together with Browaeys developed defect-free, reconfigurable arrays of hundreds of atoms. These platforms produced landmark many-body observations: quantum phase transitions in Ising-type models, quantum many-body scars, topological spin liquids, and, most recently, logical qubits with error-corrected operations. Starting from an exotic property of highly excited atoms, the nominees created a new paradigm in which atoms are positioned one by one and coupled at will, uniting atomic physics, condensed-matter physics and quantum information science. Rydberg-atom arrays are now among the leading platforms for analogue quantum simulation and scalable quantum computing worldwide.
